LE delivery and fueling operations at airports would include receiving the fuel from off-airport production or liquefaction plants, storing in insulated tanks, managing boil-off gas, and delivering the liquid to aircraft through either mobile refuelers or fixed infrastructure pipelines. Energy/fuel operations would also include continuous thermal management. LE naturally warms and vaporizes; thus, handling systems must maintain pressure/temperature stability, vent, or reliquefy boil-off to ensure safe flow through cryogenic pumps or pressure-driven systems. The flammability range for ethane is wide, and its vapor is heavier than air. These properties raise several ground-level accumulation concerns. As such, ventilation, leak detection, and controlled operating zones become a significant part of day-to- day operations. The NFPA 59A, NFPA 55, and ISO 6578 provide safety standards for safely handling, storing, and transporting LE (NFPA 2026b, 2023; ISO 2025). The NFPA 59A provides detailed safety requirements with respect to the design, construction, location and operation of facilities that deal in LNG and similar cryogenic hydrocarbons, as stated in Section 4.3.2.1. The NFPA 55 code complements the NFPA 59A code by providing general safety practices for storage, use and handling and cryogenic fluids. The safety practices in NFPA 55 cover ventilation rates in storage areas; separation distances; piping systems; containment; tank configurations; and hazard communication in order to minimize hazards of fire, explosion, or exposure. NFPA 52 (NFPA 2026c), which governs LNG and compressed natural gas fueling systems in vehicle systems, can also be used as a surrogate for LE in the absence of a relevant standard or until the establishment of a relevant code. In addition to these operational and safety standards, ISO 6578 describes a precise method for determining the mass and volume of refrigerated hydrocarbon liquids utilizing measured temperature, density, and tank conditions for accuracy in inventory management. These standards help ensure consistency in safe and reliable operations throughout facilities dealing in LE. 82 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. Due to the absence of reliable, infrastructure spatial footprint data for LE, Liquified Petroleum Gas fire code NFPA 58 (NFPA 2024a) is used as a surrogate for estimates. As a representative case, consider an aboveground storage tank with a capacity of 4500 kg requiring a minimum separation distance of 75 ft (23 m) from buildings and property lines according to NFPA 58 (NFPA 2024a). A tank of this capacity corresponds to approximately 8.3 m³ of liquid fuel using liquid ethane density of 540 kg/m³. To estimate the facility footprint, the required separation distance can be applied around the tank. A typical aboveground cryogenic storage tank of this capacity has a representative diameter of approximately 1.4 m (4.6 ft). The required footprint side length is estimated to be 47.4 m (155 ft).
